sotah-13b-26-26.note: The Roman government sent word to its garrison at Beth Peor: show us where Moses is buried. When the men stood on the upper part of the mountain, the grave seemed to be below; when they stood below, it seemed to be above. They split into two groups, and still those above saw it below and those below saw it above. So the verse was fulfilled: "no man knows of his grave to this day."
sotah-13b-26-26.why: Rabbi Berekhya has just pointed out that the Torah describes Moses' burial place very precisely and yet says no one knows it. This story shows that even with the location in hand, the grave could not be found.

terms.meaning: A place in the land of Moab; the Torah says Moses was buried in the valley opposite it.
A post of soldiers stationed in a place.

sotah-20a-8-14.note: Rabbi Meir recalled that while studying with Rabbi Akiva he used to add iron sulfate to the ink he wrote Torah scrolls with, and Rabbi Akiva said nothing. When he came to study with Rabbi Yishmael, Rabbi Yishmael asked his trade, and on hearing he was a scribe warned him to be careful, since leaving out or adding a single letter could destroy the whole world. Rabbi Meir replied that he put iron sulfate into his ink. Rabbi Yishmael objected: the Torah says the curses of the sota scroll are to be blotted out, so the writing must be erasable.
sotah-20a-8-14.why: The mishna has just described the woman suspected of adultery drinking the water into which the scroll's curses are blotted; the Gemara opens with this exchange over ink that cannot be erased, then raises a version with the teachers reversed.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: A scribe of Torah scrolls who tells of studying with two teachers.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: One of Rabbi Meir's teachers, who did not object to his ink.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael
people.about: Another teacher of Rabbi Meir, who warned him about his work and his ink.

terms.meaning: A substance added to ink to make the writing permanent so it cannot be washed off.
A wife suspected of adultery. In the Temple rite, curses were written on a scroll and dissolved in water that she drank.
One who writes Torah scrolls and other sacred texts by hand, where every letter must be exact.

sotah-21a-16-16.note: Rav Dimi reported that Hillel and Shevna were brothers. Hillel devoted himself to Torah study and stayed poor, while Shevna went into business and grew rich. In the end Shevna said to Hillel: come, let us join together and divide, offering half his wealth for half the reward of Hillel's study. A Divine Voice went out and said: "If a man would give all the fortune of his house for love, he would utterly be condemned."
sotah-21a-16-16.why: Ulla explains that this verse is not about people like those who supported a scholar from the start; it is about someone like Shevna, who tried to buy a share of Torah study after the fact.

people.name: Hillel
people.about: A brother who devoted himself to Torah and remained poor.

people.name: Shevna
people.about: Hillel's brother, a wealthy businessman who offered to trade wealth for a share in his merit.

people.name: Rav Dimi
people.about: The Sage who brought this report to Babylonia.

terms.meaning: A voice from Heaven that the Sages describe announcing a message or a ruling.

sotah-22a-9-9.note: There was a widow who had a synagogue in her own neighborhood, yet every day she came to pray in Rabbi Yohanan's study hall. Rabbi Yohanan said to her: My daughter, is there not a synagogue near you? She answered: My teacher, do I not get a reward for the steps?
sotah-22a-9-9.why: A teaching lists a widow who keeps visiting neighbors among those who erode the world. The Gemara challenges this with Rabbi Yohanan's saying that he learned about earning reward from a widow; this is that widow.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A Sage in whose study hall the widow prayed.

people.name: the widow
people.about: A woman who walked past her local synagogue to pray farther away.

terms.meaning: A house of Torah study, where prayers were also held.
The idea that each step taken on the way to a commandment, such as prayer, earns its own reward.

sotah-22b-5-5.note: Before his death, King Yannai told his wife: do not fear the Pharisees, nor those who are not Pharisees, but the hypocrites who look like Pharisees, whose deeds are like those of Zimri and who ask for a reward like that of Pinehas.
sotah-22b-5-5.why: The Gemara is going through a list of kinds of false, showy piety. Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak has just said that the heavenly court will punish those who wear the cloak of the righteous, and Yannai's warning makes the same point.

people.name: King Yannai
people.about: A king who gave this warning to his wife.

terms.meaning: The group that followed the Sages' teaching; the king contrasts them with those who are not Pharisees.
In Numbers 25, Zimri sinned openly with a Midianite woman and Pinehas killed him, earning God's reward.

sotah-33a-7-7.note: Yohanan the High Priest heard a Divine Voice coming from the Holy of Holies, saying: the youths who went to wage war in Antokhya have been victorious. Another time, Shimon HaTzaddik heard a Divine Voice from the Holy of Holies saying: the decree the enemy meant to bring against the Temple is annulled, Gaskalgas has been killed and his decrees voided. People wrote down the time, and it matched. The voice spoke in Aramaic.
sotah-33a-7-7.why: Rabbi Yohanan had said the ministering angels do not understand Aramaic, so prayers should not be said in it. The Gemara challenges him with these Aramaic voices and answers that a Divine Voice is different, or that it was Gabriel, who knows every language.

people.name: Yohanan the High Priest
people.about: A high priest who heard a voice announcing a victory.

people.name: Shimon HaTzaddik
people.about: A sage who heard a voice announcing the enemy's death.

people.name: Gaskalgas
people.about: An enemy of the Temple (identified as Caligula) whose death was announced.

terms.meaning: A voice from Heaven that the Sages describe announcing a message.
The innermost room of the Temple, entered only by the High Priest.
The everyday language of many Jews in that era, close to Hebrew but distinct from it.

sotah-40a-5-6.note: Rabbi Abbahu used to think he was humble, until he saw Rabbi Abba of Akko let his interpreter give a reason of his own in place of the one Rabbi Abba had given, and not mind at all. Rabbi Abbahu's own humility is then shown: his interpreter's wife told Rabbi Abbahu's wife that her husband did not really need Rabbi Abbahu, and bent down to hear him only out of courtesy. When his wife repeated this, Rabbi Abbahu asked what difference it made to her: through both of them, God above would be praised.
sotah-40a-5-6.why: Rabbi Abbahu has just said he stopped reciting certain verses during the Priestly Blessing because Rabbi Abba of Akko did not; the Gemara adds his other remark about Rabbi Abba and opens a run of stories about his humility.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: A leading Sage of Caesarea in the Land of Israel, with ties to the Roman authorities.

people.name: Rabbi Abba of Akko
people.about: A Sage whom Rabbi Abbahu admired for his humility.

terms.meaning: At a public lecture the Sage spoke quietly to an interpreter, who stood and repeated or expanded his words aloud for the crowd.

sotah-40a-8-9.note: Rabbi Abbahu and Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba came to the same place. Rabbi Abbahu taught stories and lore, and Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba taught law. Everyone left Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba and went to Rabbi Abbahu, and Rabbi Hiyya was offended. Rabbi Abbahu told him a parable: when one man sells precious stones and another sells small trinkets, the crowd rushes to the one with trinkets. Every day Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba used to escort Rabbi Abbahu to his lodging out of respect for the emperor's house; that day Rabbi Abbahu escorted Rabbi Hiyya to his lodging instead, and even so Rabbi Hiyya's mind was not at ease with him.
sotah-40a-8-9.why: Rabbi Abbahu has just said he once thought himself humble, and the Gemara asks what his humility was. This is one of several examples it gives.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: A Sage linked to the emperor's house, whose talks drew the crowd.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba
people.about: A Sage who taught law and was offended when his audience left.

terms.meaning: The non-legal parts of rabbinic teaching: stories, sayings and interpretations of verses.
Jewish law, and the study of its rules.

sotah-41b-2-5.note: At the public Torah reading of the Sukkot festival, the king usually received the Torah scroll standing and read it sitting. King Agrippa stood, received it and read standing, and the Sages praised him. When he reached the verse "You may not appoint a foreigner over you", tears flowed from his eyes, because he came from the house of Herod and was not of Jewish origin, and the whole people told him: you are our brother. A teaching in the name of Rabbi Natan says that at that moment the Jewish people were sentenced to destruction for flattering Agrippa. Along the way the Gemara asks how a king could sit in the Temple courtyard, answering that it was the women's courtyard, and why the Sages praised a king for giving up his honor, answering that a commandment is different.
sotah-41b-2-5.why: The Gemara is working through the mishna's account of the king's Torah reading at the Sukkot assembly. Rabbi Natan's comment then leads the discussion to the damage done by flattery.

people.name: King Agrippa
people.about: A king of Herod's house who read the Torah standing at the assembly.

people.name: Rabbi Natan
people.about: A Sage who taught that flattering Agrippa brought a sentence of destruction.

terms.meaning: An outer courtyard of the Temple, where sitting was permitted.
A polite phrase meaning the Jewish people themselves, used to avoid saying something harsh about them directly.

sotah-47a-11-13.note: When King Yannai was killing the Sages, Shimon ben Shatah was hidden by his sister, the king's wife, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Perahya fled to Alexandria in Egypt. Once peace was made, Shimon ben Shatah wrote to him as if Jerusalem were writing to Alexandria: my husband dwells with you and I sit desolate. On the way home, at an inn, the rabbi praised the place, and his student Jesus the Nazarene remarked that the innkeeper's wife had narrow eyes. Calling him wicked, the rabbi excommunicated him and turned him away day after day; when he finally signaled during Shema that he would take him back, Jesus thought he was rejected, set up a brick and worshipped it, and would not repent, citing his teacher's own rule.
sotah-47a-11-13.why: Elisha's failed attempt to bring back Gehazi has just been told, and Gehazi answered with the same rule about one who makes the masses sin. Both are teachers who pushed a student away, and the Gemara follows with the teaching that the left hand should push away while the right draws near.

people.name: Yehoshua ben Perahya
people.about: A Sage who fled to Alexandria and later excommunicated his student Jesus.

people.name: Shimon ben Shatah
people.about: A Sage hidden by his sister, King Yannai's wife, who wrote to recall Yehoshua ben Perahya.

people.name: King Yannai
people.about: The king who was killing the Sages.

people.name: Jesus the Nazarene
people.about: A student of Yehoshua ben Perahya, excommunicated by him.

terms.meaning: Rams' horns. Here four hundred were brought out as part of a formal, public excommunication.
Placed under a ban that cut the person off from the community and from his teacher.
The declaration of God's oneness, recited morning and evening, which one does not interrupt to speak.

sotah-48a-3-4.note: Yohanan the High Priest sent messengers throughout the Land of Israel and found that people set aside only the main priestly gift from their produce, while some gave the first and second tithes and some did not. He told them that eating produce without the tithe of the tithe taken, or untithed produce, carries a penalty of death at the hand of Heaven, just as with the main gift. He then made an ordinance: anyone who buys produce from an unlearned person must set aside the first and second tithes himself. The tithe of the tithe goes to a priest and the second tithe is eaten in Jerusalem, but the Levite and the poor cannot demand their shares without proof.
sotah-48a-3-4.why: The mishna says Yohanan the High Priest abolished the declaration of tithes; the Gemara had explained that people gave the tithe to priests rather than Levites, and this account, showing many did not tithe at all, challenges that, leading to the answer that he made two separate ordinances.

people.name: Yohanan the High Priest
people.about: He investigated tithing across the land and instituted the ordinance on doubtfully tithed produce.

terms.meaning: The main gift from a harvest that must be given to a priest before the produce may be eaten.
Tenths of produce: the first tithe goes to the Levites, who give a tenth of it to priests; the second tithe is eaten by its owner in Jerusalem; the poor man's tithe goes to the poor.
An unlearned person, who could not be trusted to have set aside the required tithes.
Produce bought from someone who may not have tithed it; Yohanan's decree requires the buyer to tithe it.

sotah-48a-17-17.note: Rav Huna taught that the songs of men hauling ships or leading herds are permitted, but the singing of weavers is forbidden. Later Rav Huna banned all song, and food became so plentiful that a hundred ducks, or a hundred se'a of wheat, sold for a dinar and no one wanted them. Then Rav Hisda came and made light of the ban, and afterward a single duck could not be found even for a dinar.
sotah-48a-17-17.why: The mishna says song was banned after the Sanhedrin ceased, and Rav and Rava have just warned that song in a house brings its ruin. Rav Huna's ban, and what happened when it lapsed, illustrates that warning in prices.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A Sage who first permitted work songs and later banned all song.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: A Sage who came after and made light of Rav Huna's ban.

terms.meaning: A measure of volume for grain, roughly several liters.
A silver coin; a hundred ducks for one dinar means food was almost free.

sotah-48b-6-8.note: Once the Sages were reclining in an upper room of the house of Gurya in Jericho when a Divine Voice announced that one of them was worthy of the Divine Presence resting on him, but his generation was not fit for it. They looked at Hillel the Elder, and when he died they eulogized him: Alas pious one, alas humble one, student of Ezra. The same thing happened in Yavne, and they looked at Shmuel HaKatan, mourned as a student of Hillel. As he was dying, Shmuel HaKatan foretold that Shimon and Yishmael would go to the sword, their colleagues to killing and the people to plunder. The Sages wanted to eulogize Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava the same way, but the times were too troubled, since those killed by the monarchy were not eulogized.
sotah-48b-6-8.why: A baraita has just said that after Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi died the Divine Spirit left Israel, but the Sages still received guidance through a Divine Voice. These scenes are its proof.

people.name: Hillel the Elder
people.about: The Sage the others looked to in Jericho, eulogized as a student of Ezra.

people.name: Shmuel HaKatan
people.about: The Sage singled out in Yavne, eulogized as a student of Hillel; he foretold coming killings.

people.name: Shimon
people.about: Named by Shmuel HaKatan as destined for the sword; the translation identifies him as Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

people.name: Yishmael
people.about: Named with Shimon as destined for the sword; the translation identifies him as Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha the High Priest.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava
people.about: A Sage killed by the monarchy, whom the Sages could not eulogize.

terms.meaning: A voice from Heaven that the Sages heard after prophecy had ended.
God's presence resting on a person, the mark of a prophet.

sotah-49a-9-9.note: Rav Huna found a fragrant date and wrapped it in his shawl. His son Rabba came in and said he could smell a fragrant date. Rav Huna told him, My son, there is purity in you, and gave it to him. Then Rabba's own son Abba arrived, and Rabba gave the date to him. Rav Huna said to Rabba: My son, you have made my heart rejoice and you have blunted my teeth. The Gemara adds the folk saying that a father's love goes to his sons, and the sons' love to their own sons.
sotah-49a-9-9.why: The mishna said that since the Temple was destroyed fruit has lost its taste, and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar has just taught that lost purity took away taste and aroma. Rabba's ability to smell the date is read as a sign of that purity.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: The father who found the date and gave it to his son.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Rav Huna's son, who smelled the date and gave it to his own son.

people.name: Abba
people.about: Rabba's son, who received the date.

terms.meaning: An expression of hurt: Rav Huna was pained that his son passed the gift to the grandson rather than back to him.

sotah-49a-10-10.note: Rav Aha bar Yaakov raised Rav Yaakov, his daughter's son. When the boy had grown up, his grandfather asked him for a drink of water, and the grandson answered: I am not your son. The Gemara attaches the folk saying: raise him, raise him, and he will say, I am your daughter's son.
sotah-49a-10-10.why: It follows directly on the story of Rav Huna, his son and grandson, which ended with a saying that a son's love goes to his own sons. This second incident adds a saying about how a grandchild repays the grandparent who raised him.

people.name: Rav Aha bar Yaakov
people.about: A Sage who raised his daughter's son.

people.name: Rav Yaakov
people.about: Rav Aha bar Yaakov's grandson, who refused him water once grown.

sotah-49b-4-4.note: Rabba bar Rav Huna made a tambourine for his son. His father, Rav Huna, came and broke it, saying it could be confused with a one-mouthed drum. He told him to make one instead over the mouth of an earthen jug or of a small kefiza measuring vessel.
sotah-49b-4-4.why: The mishna lists a decree against drums from the war of Vespasian, and Rabbi Elazar has just defined that drum as one with a single mouth. Rav Huna's act shows the ban applied even to a toy that might look like one.

people.name: Rabba bar Rav Huna
people.about: Made a tambourine for his son.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Rabba's father, who broke the tambourine.

terms.meaning: A drum with a skin on one side only, the instrument the Sages banned.
A small unit of measure; here, the small vessel used to measure it, over which a toy drum could be made.

sotah-49b-7-9.note: When the Hasmonean kings fought each other, Hyrcanus besieged Jerusalem with Aristobulus inside. Each day those inside lowered coins in a box, and those outside sent up animals for the daily Temple offerings. An elder who knew Greek wisdom told the besiegers, in that Greek wisdom, that as long as the Temple service went on the city would not fall to them. The next day they sent up a pig. Halfway up the wall it dug in its hooves, and the land of Israel shook for four hundred parasangs. At that time the Sages said: cursed is one who raises pigs, and cursed is one who teaches his son Greek wisdom. That year the omer had to come from Gaggot Tzerifim and the two loaves from the valley of Ein Sokher.
sotah-49b-7-9.why: The mishna lists a decree that a man may not teach his son Greek, and this baraita gives its origin. The Gemara then asks how that fits with Sages who praised the Greek language, and answers that the language and Greek wisdom are separate things.

people.name: Hyrcanus
people.about: A Hasmonean king, besieging Jerusalem from outside.

people.name: Aristoblus
people.about: A Hasmonean king, besieged inside Jerusalem.

terms.meaning: The two lambs offered in the Temple every day, morning and afternoon.
A Persian measure of distance, a few miles.
The measure of barley offered in the Temple on the second day of Passover.
The two wheat loaves offered in the Temple on Shavuot.
